title: Does Qualifying Position Predict F1 Race Results? 🏎️
text:
In Formula 1, race day gets all the glory, but Sunday’s results are heavily shaped on Saturday afternoon during qualifying. Securing a spot at the front of the starting grid grants clear air, lower tire degradation, and a massive strategic advantage. But how strong is that relationship in reality? Does starting on pole position practically guarantee a victory, or do race-day chaos, safety cars, and brilliant recovery drives disrupt the grid order?
In this tutorial, we will use pandas to load, clean, and visualize historical Formula 1 data to explore whether a driver’s qualifying position predicts their final race finish. By the end of this post, you will be able to handle real-world tabular data, compute performance shifts, and build an informative scatter plot using Python.

The Dataset
To answer our question, we will utilize the comprehensive Formula 1 World Championship (1950 - 2024) Dataset. This dataset contains rich relational tables covering race results, qualifying sessions, lap times, and driver details. Specifically, we are interested in comparing the grid column (starting position) against the positionOrder column (final race finish).

text:
Loading and Cleaning Data with Pandas
First, let’s load our data using pandas and inspect the core structure of our dataframes.

import pandas as pd

# Load the qualifying and race results datasets
results_df = pd.read_csv("data/results.csv")
qualifying_df = pd.read_csv("data/qualifying.csv")

# Preview the columns to understand how they align
print(results_df.head())
print(qualifying_df.head())

When analyzing the relationship between starting grid position and final race position, it helps to frame the expectation mathematically. We can model the expected finishing position using a simple linear relationship:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i\]
Where \(X_i\) represents the starting grid position of driver \(i\), \(Y_i\) represents their final race finish position, \(\beta_0\) is the baseline intercept, \(\beta_1\) measures the predictive strength of qualifying, and \(\epsilon_i\) accounts for race-day variance and unmeasured factors.

title: Does Qualifying Position Predict F1 Race Results? 🏎️
text:
Visualizing the Relationship
To truly understand how predictive qualifying is across hundreds of historical races, visualization is essential. Let’s write a snippet using matplotlib and seaborn to plot grid positions against final race finishes.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd

# Load data and filter for 2024
races_df = pd.read_csv("data/races.csv")
drivers_df = pd.read_csv("data/drivers.csv")

df_merged = results_df.merge(races_df[['raceId', 'year']], on='raceId') \
                      .merge(drivers_df[['driverId', 'surname']], on='driverId')

df_2024 = df_merged[df_merged['year'] == 2024].dropna(subset=['grid', 'positionOrder'])
df_2024 = df_2024[(df_2024['grid'] > 0) & (df_2024['positionOrder'] <= 20)]

# Calculate positions gained/lost (Grid minus Finish: positive means gained positions)
df_2024['gained'] = df_2024['grid'] - df_2024['positionOrder']

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

# Plot lines colored by performance change (gained/lost)
for _, row in df_2024.iterrows():
    # Highlight major movers (gained 3+ positions in green, lost 3+ in orange, rest neutral gray)
    if row['gained'] >= 3:
        color, alpha, zorder = '#2ecc71', 0.6, 3 # Green for strong climbers
    elif row['gained'] <= -3:
        color, alpha, zorder = '#e74c3c', 0.4, 2 # Red/Orange for droppers
    else:
        color, alpha, zorder = '#bdc3c7', 0.15, 1 # Neutral gray for steady results
        
    plt.plot([1, 2], [row['grid'], row['positionOrder']], color=color, alpha=alpha, zorder=zorder, linewidth=1.5)

plt.title("2024 F1 Race Day Shifts: Who Climbed the Grid?", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.xticks([1, 2], ['Qualifying Grid', 'Race Finish'], fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel("Position", fontsize=12)
plt.yticks(range(1, 21))
plt.gca().invert_yaxis() # 1st place at the top
plt.grid(True, axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








By examining the 2024 season scatter plot, you will notice a dense clustering along the diagonal line, indicating that qualifying position is indeed a strong predictor. However, you will also spot significant spread where drivers drop back due to mechanical failures or surge forward through stellar overtaking performances.

text:
Conclusion and Next Steps
Our exploratory analysis confirms that while qualifying is a vital indicator of race success, Formula 1 remains wonderfully unpredictable on Sundays. Fast qualifiers have a massive statistical advantage, but strategy, tire management, and weather always play a deciding role.
Call to Action: Try tweaking the script to filter for a different season (like 2023 or 2022) to see how the grid-to-finish relationship changes across different regulatory eras!
